title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed analysis of the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey finds US small firms using AI are markedly more optimistic on next-year hiring (+33 vs +15 net) and revenue (+48 vs +21 net) than non-users, with gaps of 10-14 points surviving controls. The premium is largest among financially weaker firms and those with technology challenges, suggesting AI eases operational constraints rather than reflecting owner optimism.

insights.claim: In the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey, 46% of US employer small firms said their business or employees were using AI tools, and another 15% planned to adopt within twelve months.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: Roughly 6 in 10 small employers are using or about to use AI, so AI diffusion is already mainstream in the small-business segment, not confined to large corporates.
insights.quote: 46 percent of firms with at least one employee stated that their business or employees were using AI tools, with another 15 percent planning to adopt them in the next twelve months
insights.locator: In the SBCS report on findings

insights.claim: Among small-business AI users, 63% say AI is somewhat or very important to production and 51% have partially or fully integrated AI into business processes.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: Adoption is moving beyond experimentation toward operational integration for about half of users.
insights.quote: among AI users, 63 percent said that AI was somewhat or very important to production and 51 percent had integrated AI partially or fully
insights.locator: In the SBCS report on findings

insights.claim: Small businesses may lack staff, expertise and resources to deploy AI, but may face fewer coordination challenges than large firms when integrating it; the concurrent surge in business startups alongside AI adoption hints AI may be a positive force for small firms.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: Small firms could be relative beneficiaries of AI because of low integration friction, supporting the startup-formation boom.
insights.quote: the concurrent surge in national business startups with the growing adoption of AI suggests that these tools may be a positive force for small businesses
insights.locator: AI Use by Large and Small Businesses

themes.theme: AI users expect more hiring, not less

insights.claim: There is little consensus on AI's employment effect: economy-wide pay and headcount have barely moved despite rapid AI adoption, while narrower measures show declining hiring for early-career workers and AI-exposed occupations.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: Aggregate labor data may mask concentrated displacement among entry-level and exposed occupations; small-business data offers a different lens.
insights.quote: Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly

insights.claim: Small employer firms currently using AI had a +33 percentage point net expectation of higher employment over the next twelve months, versus +15 points for non-users.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: At the small-business level, AI adoption is associated with hiring intentions rather than job cuts, contrary to the displacement narrative.
insights.quote: those who currently use AI had a 33 percentage point net expectation of higher employment in the next twelve months, while non-users had only a 15 percentage point net expectation

insights.claim: 77% of small-business respondents reported no change in current labor costs from using AI.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: So far AI is not visibly substituting labor costs at small firms, consistent with limited aggregate labor-market effects.
insights.quote: 77 percent of respondents reported no change in their firm’s current labor costs from the use of AI

insights.claim: After controlling for owner demographics, firm characteristics and location, AI users' net probability of expected employment growth remains 13 percentage points higher than non-users'; adding past twelve-month employment changes still leaves a 10-point gap.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: The AI-hiring-optimism link is robust to obvious confounders, strengthening the case that AI is complementary to small-firm employment.
insights.quote: the net probability of expected employment growth remains higher for AI users than for non-users (by 13 percentage points

insights.claim: Younger and more profitable firms, and those with more than ten employees, are likelier to hold optimistic employment expectations, and past employment changes correlate with expected future changes.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: Firm age, profitability, size and momentum are confounders that must be stripped out before attributing hiring optimism to AI.
insights.quote: we find that younger and more profitable firms—and those with more than ten employees—are likelier to have more optimistic employment expectations
insights.locator: Firm expectations could be explained by

insights.claim: Among AI users, firms with AI fully or partially integrated, or that see AI as important to production, are no more likely to expect higher employment than firms merely experimenting with AI, after controls.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: Deeper AI integration does not translate into extra hiring optimism, suggesting the employment link is not a simple dose-response effect.
insights.quote: are equally likely to expect higher relative to lower employment compared to those who are experimenting with AI
insights.locator: Among AI users, those who report

insights.claim: Using self-reported financial condition as an optimism proxy, the AI-user employment-expectation premium is larger among firms in fair or poor condition (+21 points) than among those in good or better condition (+10 points), the opposite of what a spurious optimism story predicts.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: AI's association with hiring intentions is strongest at weaker firms, implying AI may be a remedy for struggling businesses rather than a marker of already-optimistic owners.
insights.quote: the net probability of expected employment growth is 21 percentage points higher for AI users than for non-users, while the difference is only 10 percentage points among owners reporting good or better conditions

insights.claim: For revenue, the AI-user premium is 24 percentage points among firms in fair or poor financial condition versus 15 points for firms in good condition, both statistically significant, leading the authors to judge a spurious AI-revenue association unlikely.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: Reinforces that AI benefits, as perceived by owners, accrue disproportionately to weaker small firms.
insights.quote: it seems unlikely that the association between AI use and positive revenue expectations is spurious

insights.claim: Only 31% of small-business respondents reported increased sales from their use of AI.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: Realized AI revenue gains remain a minority experience, so forward optimism outruns current measurable payoff.
insights.quote: Only 31 percent of survey respondents reported increased sales from their firm’s use of AI

insights.claim: Among small employer firms using AI, the net share expecting higher revenue next year is +48 percentage points, versus +21 points for non-users.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: AI adopters anticipate materially stronger top-line growth, a potential leading indicator for small-business activity.
insights.quote: the share expecting revenues to increase exceeded the share expecting them to decrease by 48 percentage points, compared with only 21 percentage points among non-users

insights.claim: After controlling for firm and owner characteristics and past twelve-month revenue changes, AI users retain a 14 percentage point advantage in net expected revenue growth.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: The revenue-optimism premium for AI users survives controls, mirroring the employment result.
insights.quote: AI users still have a 14 percentage point advantage over non-users in net expected revenue growth

insights.claim: AI users facing operational challenges in utilizing technology (website, social media, ecommerce, cybersecurity) have a 16 percentage point higher net revenue-growth expectation than AI users without such challenges, suggesting AI helps firms overcome internal technological constraints.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: AI's value to small firms may come mainly from filling tech-capability gaps, favoring AI tools aimed at non-technical SMB operations.
insights.quote: AI may improve revenue expectations by helping firms overcome internal technological constraints that would otherwise limit growth

insights.claim: The authors conclude AI appears to help some small businesses overcome specific operational or technical constraints on revenue, rather than reflecting broad optimism or hiring-led expansion; whether expected gains materialize is left for future research.
insights.speaker: Will Aarons
insights.so_what: Findings are expectations-based, not realized outcomes; investors should treat them as sentiment evidence pending hard data.
insights.quote: Whether AI-adopting firms actually experience the stronger revenue and employment outcomes they anticipate is a subject for future research
